person.name: Elena Cruz
person.traits: Composed and calculating. Switches quickly from denial to negotiation when cornered.

start.prompt: The floor goes quiet as you walk through it. Forty headsets. Forty scripts in plastic sleeves. A woman in a blazer steps out of the back room, phone already in her hand. "I don't know what Marco told you, but whatever it was, it's not the whole story."

choices.text: It's enough to shut this place down. Marco already gave us the details.
Forty desks. Say the number of people out loud for me.

scale_node.prompt: She doesn't blink. "They're employees. They have quotas, like anybody else." Behind her, a laminated card taped to a monitor reads: [i]IF THEY HESITATE, REMIND THEM OF THE DEADLINE.[/i] Not a suggestion. A procedure.

choices.text: That card isn't sales. It's a method for getting past somebody's judgment.

pressure_node.prompt: "You don't want to do this," she says, lowering her voice. "I can make this a very expensive mistake for you."

choices.text: Are you offering me money to walk away?
I'm not interested in whatever you're about to say. This ends today.

bribe_offer.prompt: "Let's just call it... an inconvenience fee." She names a number that would change your life. "Nobody in this room is going to remember this conversation any differently than you do."

choices.text: Take the money and end the investigation here.

tactic_quiz.setup: You think about two of the people this floor called. Maria Santos, sixty-seven, a retired clerk, told her account would be frozen unless she verified right now. Kevin Dizon, twenty-four, works with computers all day, told his files were infected and to call before restarting.
tactic_quiz.question: Two completely different scripts, two completely different people. What did both scripts actually need in order to work?

milestone.title: The Pattern Named
milestone.detail: Identified that every script in the operation depended on removing the victim's time to verify - not on the victim being careless, old, or bad with technology.

options.text: A reason to act right away, before checking with anybody else.
options.feedback: That is the whole operation in one sentence. Every script - bank, tech support, raffle - is built to close the gap between hearing the story and acting on it. The defense is always the same, and it is boring: stop, hang up, and check through a number you already trust. Nothing real is ever lost by waiting ten minutes.

options.text: A victim who wasn't very good with technology.
options.feedback: Look at who they actually hit. Maria handled money for a living for thirty years. Kevin is twenty-four and works on computers every day. The idea that only gullible people fall for this is not just wrong - it is useful to the operation, because people who think they are immune don't check, and people who feel stupid don't report.

Spoofed numbers help, and they are easy to fake - which is why caller ID should never be treated as proof of anything. But a perfect fake number still fails against somebody who hangs up and calls back on their own. The time pressure is what stops them doing that.

options.text: The victim's bank details, obtained in advance.
options.feedback: They had almost nothing in advance. Both scripts were designed to make the victim hand over what was missing. The pressure is not there to use the information - it is there to get it.

end_bribed.prompt: You walk out with a number in your account and a case that quietly goes nowhere. Marco's statement sits in a drawer, unopened. The forty headsets are back on by Monday, working a list that now has more names on it, with notes in the margin. Somewhere, the witnesses who trusted you are still waiting for a call that is never coming.

milestone.title: Investigation Compromised
milestone.detail: The lead investigator accepted a bribe instead of closing the case.

end_full_takedown.prompt: By evening, officers move through three floors of the building, and then a fourth door with a card reader on it. Scripts, victim lists, payment logs and two leases are seized, and the leases carry a signature. With a second confirmed testimony behind Marco's statement and the name above the floors in your file, there is enough to charge {company} - the man who signed for the building, not just the people who read the scripts in it. The lists are the part that matters: every name on them belongs to someone who was going to be called again.

milestone.title: Investigation Breakthrough
milestone.detail: Enough evidence was gathered to bring down the operation, not just the individual callers.

end_building_stands.prompt: By evening, officers move through both call floors. Scripts, victim lists and payment logs are seized; Marco, Elena and the desks face charges. But the floors are leased, and the leases are in a holding company's name, and nobody on either floor can say who signs for it - the fifth floor has a card reader and no name on the door. The building stands. So does whoever owns it, and the lease on the next floor is already being drawn up.

milestone.title: The Floors Fall, The Building Stands
milestone.detail: Both call floors were taken down on the strength of the witnesses - but nobody inside the building had named its owner, and an owner who is never named leases the next floor.

end_partial_justice.prompt: The raid takes in Marco and the desks that worked the one script you could prove. But every statement in your file tells the same story, and one story is one desk's work, not an operation's - the other scripts on that floor were never put on record, so the people who wrote them slip through the paperwork. Those scripts survive. So do the lists. Some justice, not all of it.
